questions.question: What is Amazon EFS and what makes it different from Amazon EBS?
questions.answer: Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system. The key difference from EBS: EFS can be mounted by thousands of EC2 instances simultaneously (shared), scales automatically, and is multi-AZ by default. EBS attaches to one instance at a time, requires provisioning a fixed size, and is confined to a single AZ.

questions.question: What protocol does EFS use and what port must be open?
questions.answer: EFS uses NFSv4 (Network File System version 4). Port 2049 must be allowed in security groups — inbound on the mount target's security group from EC2 instances, and outbound from the EC2 security group to port 2049.

questions.question: What is a mount target in EFS?
questions.answer: A mount target is an NFS endpoint (with its own IP address and DNS name) created in a specific Availability Zone within your VPC. EC2 instances connect to the mount target in their AZ to access the EFS file system. Best practice is to create one mount target per AZ you want to use.

questions.question: Which operating systems does EFS support?
questions.answer: EFS is Linux-only. It uses the POSIX standard (Unix/Linux file permissions and directory structure) and NFSv4 protocol, which are Linux concepts. For Windows EC2 instances needing shared file storage, use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server instead.

questions.question: What are the two EFS performance modes?
questions.answer: General Purpose (default) — optimized for the lowest per-operation latency; best for most workloads like web servers, CMS, home directories. Max I/O — optimized for maximum aggregate throughput with slightly higher latency; best for massively parallel workloads with hundreds of EC2 instances. Cannot be changed after file system creation.

questions.question: What is EFS Standard-IA and when would you use it?
questions.answer: EFS Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) stores data across multiple AZs at significantly lower cost than EFS Standard, but charges a per-request retrieval fee when files are read. Use it for files not accessed frequently — compliance archives, old logs, rarely-touched configuration files. Enable lifecycle management to automatically move files to IA based on last-access time.

questions.question: How does EFS pricing work?
questions.answer: EFS charges per GB of data actually stored per month. There is no provisioning and no minimum fee. Different storage classes have different rates — Standard is most expensive, One Zone-IA is cheapest. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA also add per-request retrieval fees when files are read.

questions.question: What is the difference between EFS One Zone and EFS Standard storage classes?
questions.answer: EFS Standard stores data across multiple Availability Zones — high availability and durability but higher cost. EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ — lower cost (roughly 47% less) but data is at risk if that AZ experiences an outage. One Zone is suitable for dev/test or data that can be recreated; Standard is required for production data needing HA.

questions.question: What does the _netdev option do in /etc/fstab for EFS?
questions.answer: _netdev tells the Linux operating system to defer mounting this file system until the network is available. Without it, the EC2 instance may try to mount EFS before the network interface is ready at boot, causing the instance to get stuck or fail to start properly. This is essential for cloud environments where storage mounts depend on network connectivity.

questions.question: What is EFS lifecycle management and what does it do?
questions.answer: EFS lifecycle management automatically moves files between Standard and IA storage classes based on how recently they were accessed. You configure a threshold (e.g., move files not accessed in 30 days to Standard-IA). Files are automatically moved back to Standard when accessed. This can save up to 92% on storage costs for infrequently accessed files with no manual effort.

questions.question: A web application has 10 EC2 instances behind a load balancer. Users upload profile photos. After upload, the photo isn't visible on subsequent page loads. Diagnose and fix the problem.
questions.answer: (Situation) Photos uploaded to one EC2 instance aren't visible when requests hit a different instance. (Task) Fix shared file availability. (Action) Identified root cause: each instance uses its own local EBS volume for storage — no sharing. Implemented: created an EFS file system, mounted it on all 10 instances at the same path (/var/app/uploads), updated the application config to use that path. (Result) All uploads are now written to EFS, readable by all instances immediately regardless of which server handles the request.

questions.question: EFS mount is failing on a new EC2 instance. The file system exists and is active. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: (Situation) EFS mount fails on new EC2 instance. (Task) Systematically diagnose. (Action) Checked in order: 1) Is port 2049 open in the mount target's security group (inbound from EC2 SG)? — found it was missing. 2) Is the EC2 in the same VPC as the mount target? 3) Is the NFS client installed (nfs-utils / nfs-common)? 4) Is the mount command using the correct EFS DNS name and NFSv4 options? Added port 2049 inbound rule. (Result) Mount succeeded immediately after adding the security group rule.

questions.question: A company's EFS storage costs are growing unexpectedly. An audit shows 85% of files haven't been accessed in 90+ days. What do you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) High EFS costs due to inactive files. (Task) Reduce cost without deleting data. (Action) Enabled EFS lifecycle management with a 30-day threshold: any file not accessed in 30 days moves automatically to Standard-IA (reduces storage cost by ~92% for those files). Files in IA are still accessible on demand — retrieved automatically and moved back to Standard when accessed. (Result) Monthly EFS costs projected to drop by ~78% (85% of files at 92% discount) with no application code changes or data loss.

questions.question: You need to mount EFS across multiple microservices, but each microservice should only access its own data directory even though they share the same file system. How do you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Multiple microservices, single EFS, need per-app isolation. (Task) Implement directory-level isolation. (Action) Created EFS Access Points — one per microservice. Each access point configured with: a specific root directory (/service-a, /service-b, etc.) and a POSIX user (UID/GID matching the microservice's container user). Updated ECS/EKS task definitions to mount EFS via the specific access point. (Result) Each microservice sees only its own directory, runs as its designated user, and cannot access other services' files — secure multi-tenant sharing on a single file system.

questions.question: A customer wants to migrate their on-premises NFS file server (10TB of data) to AWS with minimal application changes. What do you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) Legacy NFS server on-premises, needs AWS migration. (Task) Migrate to AWS with minimum code changes. (Action) Recommended EFS as a drop-in NFS replacement. Plan: 1) Set up AWS Direct Connect or VPN for private connectivity; 2) Create an EFS file system sized appropriately with lifecycle management; 3) Use AWS DataSync to migrate the 10TB of data from the on-premises NFS server to EFS; 4) Update application mount configurations to point to EFS DNS instead of the old NFS server IP; 5) Test and cut over. (Result) Application is unchanged — only the NFS server endpoint changes. No code modifications required.

questions.question: What is the difference between EFS Elastic, Provisioned, and Bursting throughput modes?
questions.answer: Elastic Throughput (recommended) automatically scales up and down with your workload. Provisioned Throughput lets you specify a fixed MiB/s regardless of file system size — for workloads that consistently need more throughput than their file system size would normally allow. Bursting Throughput earns credits during idle periods and spends them for bursting — the baseline is 50 MiB/s per TiB of storage. Choose Elastic for variable workloads, Provisioned for consistently high-throughput small file systems, and Bursting only for predictable burst patterns.

questions.question: How does EFS encryption at rest differ from encryption in transit, and how do you enable each?
questions.answer: These are completely separate protections. Encryption at rest: enabled at file system creation time using a KMS key — cannot be enabled after creation. Encrypts all data stored on EFS. Encryption in transit: enabled at mount time using TLS. With amazon-efs-utils: mount -t efs -o tls fs-xxxx:/ /mnt/efs. Encrypts data moving between the EC2 instance and the EFS mount target. You can have one without the other, but best practice is to enable both.

questions.question: Can EFS be used with AWS Lambda? What are the requirements?
questions.answer: Yes — Lambda functions can mount EFS file systems. Requirements: 1) Lambda must be configured to run in a VPC; 2) The VPC must have mount targets for the EFS file system in the same subnets as the Lambda function; 3) Security groups must allow port 2049 between Lambda and the mount target; 4) The Lambda execution role needs elasticfilesystem:ClientMount (and ClientWrite) permissions. This is useful for Lambda functions that need to share state or access large files that exceed Lambda's 512MB /tmp storage limit.

questions.question: What are EFS Access Points and how do they enforce security?
questions.answer: EFS Access Points are application-specific NFS entry points into an EFS file system. Each access point enforces: 1) A root directory — connections through this access point see only this subdirectory (not the full EFS); 2) A POSIX user identity (UID/GID) — all writes are attributed to this user regardless of the actual connecting process. Combined with IAM policies that restrict which roles can use which access points, you get strong, auditable per-application isolation on shared EFS file systems without separate file systems per app.

questions.question: A development team says EFS performance is degrading as they added more concurrent users. They are on General Purpose mode. What do you investigate and potentially change?
questions.answer: (Situation) EFS performance degrading with more users. (Task) Diagnose and improve. (Action) Checked: 1) CloudWatch metrics — PercentIOLimit metric shows if they are approaching the General Purpose IOPS limit (1% of max = warning zone); 2) Found PercentIOLimit consistently above 80%. Since General Purpose has a per-operation latency limit that becomes a bottleneck with many concurrent clients, recommended migrating to Max I/O mode. Created a new EFS file system with Max I/O, migrated data using AWS DataSync. (Result) PercentIOLimit dropped significantly; performance improved with concurrent users.

questions.question: Design an EFS strategy for a three-tier web application with compliance requirements: all data must be encrypted, backed up for 7 years, and auditable.
questions.answer: Architecture: EFS file system with encryption at rest (KMS CMK with CloudTrail key usage logging). Mount with TLS for encryption in transit. Enable lifecycle management: Standard → Standard-IA after 30 days (cost optimization). For 7-year retention: enable EFS Replication to a second region for DR. Use AWS Backup to create a backup plan that retains EFS backups for 7 years with WORM (Write Once Read Many) vault lock for immutability. Enable CloudTrail for all EFS API calls. Mount via Access Points for per-application isolation. Result: fully encrypted, backed up for 7 years with immutable records, and every access audited.

questions.question: Compare Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre. When would you choose each?
questions.answer: EFS is a managed NFS file system — POSIX compliant, general-purpose, suitable for web workloads, CMS, home directories, containers, and lift-and-shift of NFS workloads. Throughput scales to GBs for general workloads. FSx for Lustre is a managed high-performance parallel file system — throughputs of hundreds of GB/s and millions of IOPS. Designed for HPC (High Performance Computing), machine learning training, financial simulations, seismic processing. It integrates natively with S3 (can directly process S3 objects). Choose EFS for general shared file needs; choose FSx for Lustre when you need sub-millisecond latency and massive parallel I/O at HPC scale.

questions.question: How would you implement high availability for an EFS-based application if an AZ goes down?
questions.answer: EFS Standard is inherently multi-AZ — data is replicated across AZs automatically. HA strategy: 1) Use EFS Standard (not One Zone); 2) Create mount targets in all AZs where your EC2 instances run; 3) Use Auto Scaling groups with instances spread across AZs (AZ rebalancing enabled); 4) Use EFS DNS name for mounting — it resolves to the nearest available mount target automatically. When an AZ fails: ASG launches replacement instances in healthy AZs; they mount EFS via mount targets in their own AZs; the EFS data is already available there. Zero recovery action needed — HA is built-in.

questions.question: What CloudWatch metrics should you monitor for EFS and what do they indicate?
questions.answer: Key EFS CloudWatch metrics: PercentIOLimit — percentage of GP mode I/O limit used; if consistently above 80%, consider migrating to Max I/O. BurstCreditBalance — remaining burst credits; if trending to zero, either switch to Elastic Throughput or increase file system size. ThroughputUtilization — percentage of provisioned throughput being used (Provisioned mode only). ClientConnections — number of NFS connections; useful for capacity planning. StorageBytes — total bytes stored, broken down by storage class. MeteredIOBytes — data transferred (billing metric). Set CloudWatch alarms on PercentIOLimit and BurstCreditBalance to proactively avoid performance degradation.

questions.question: How does AWS DataSync relate to EFS, and when would you use it?
questions.answer: AWS DataSync is a fully managed data transfer service that accelerates moving data to and from EFS (and other storage). Use cases with EFS: 1) Migration — transfer data from on-premises NFS/SMB file servers to EFS; 2) Replication — copy data between two EFS file systems (cross-region or same-region); 3) S3 to EFS — import data from S3 into EFS for processing; 4) EFS to S3 — export processed files to S3 for archival. DataSync uses parallel multi-threaded transfers, handles retries automatically, and integrates with CloudWatch for monitoring. For a 10TB migration, DataSync can complete in hours vs days for manual rsync.
